content: Ventouse is a vacuum device specifically designed to assist in the delivery of a baby when labor has not progressed adequately. It serves as an alternative to forceps delivery. However, it is generally not used in cases where the baby is in the breech position or during premature births. This method is also referred to as vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery. During the procedure, the woman is positioned in the lithotomy position and actively participates by pushing throughout the process. A suction cup is applied to the baby’s head, and the vacuum creates suction that draws the skin of the scalp into the cup. Most ventouse devices are equipped with handles, allowing the practitioner to guide the baby’s head during delivery. Once the baby’s head is delivered, the device is detached, enabling the mother to complete the delivery of her child. In some cases, ventouse deliveries have been performed before the cervix is fully dilated, though there is ongoing debate among medical professionals regarding the appropriateness of this practice. If the ventouse attempt is unsuccessful, it may become necessary to deliver the baby via cesarean section. When compared to other forms of assisted delivery, ventouse has several advantages. For instance, an episiotomy is not typically required, and there is minimal internal bruising. Additionally, the mother remains actively involved in the birthing process. The force applied to the baby during a ventouse delivery is generally less than that used in a forceps delivery, which reduces the likelihood of significant markings on the baby’s head and face. However, there are also some drawbacks associated with ventouse delivery. The baby may develop a temporary swelling on the head, known as a chignon, as a result of the suction. In some cases, the baby may experience distress due to the strong suction applied to the head.
